source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Religious Studies past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: In many villages of Cameroon an elder may pour a few drops of palm wine on the ground before drinking, speaking to the ancestors and asking for the blessing of God. A single gesture shows several layers of belief at once. Examiners ask who the Supreme Being is, where the divinities come from and how the two are related, and they reward answers that explain this order carefully. This course gives the structure and shows how to avoid the mistake of treating all African peoples as holding exactly the same beliefs.

items: African Traditional Religion (ATR) is the name given to the many traditional religions of African peoples; it has no single founder and no single holy book.
Its beliefs are handed down orally through myths, proverbs, songs, rituals and the teaching of elders.
A shrine is a place set apart where people meet the spiritual world through prayer, offerings and ritual.

sections.titre: The ordered spiritual world of ATR: Supreme Being, divinities, spirits and ancestors
sections.contenu_markdown:
### A note on method
Practices and names differ from one people to another, so a good answer speaks of what believers in ATR commonly hold and uses an example from a named people only when sure of it.

### The structure of the spiritual world
Believers commonly describe an ordered world, from the highest being down to the human community.
| Level | Who or what | Role |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The Supreme Being | Creator and source of life and of all other spiritual beings |
| 2 | Divinities (lesser gods, deities) | Agents and ministers of the Supreme Being; each has a field of activity |
| 3 | Spirits | Spiritual beings linked to places, forces or persons; may help or harm |
| 4 | Ancestors (the living-dead) | Departed members of the family who still watch over it |

This ordered pattern is what is meant when the concept of divinity is called **stratified** or ranked.

### The Supreme Being
Peoples use different names: Olodumare among the Yoruba, Nyame among the Akan and Chukwu among the Igbo are well-known examples. Believers describe the Supreme Being as creator, all-powerful, all-knowing, eternal, just and beyond full human understanding. Many societies picture God as high above and approach Him mainly through intermediaries, with few shrines and priests of His own; prayer and short invocations are, however, made directly, especially in crisis. Believers also speak of God as near, caring for the world He made.

### The divinities
Believers hold that the divinities **owe their origin to the Supreme Being**: He created them or gave them their place and authority, and they act on His behalf. Many are linked to nature (the sky and thunder, the earth, rivers, hills) or to human activities such as farming, healing and the working of iron; some are explained as deified ancestors or heroes. The Yoruba orisa such as Sango, associated with thunder, are a well-known example. Divinities have shrines, priests or priestesses, festivals and offerings.

### Functions of the divinities
- To act as intermediaries between people and the Supreme Being.
- To control the forces of nature on which the community depends.
- To protect morality and order, since wrongdoing is held to offend them.
- To bring healing, fertility and protection, which explains why people consult them.

### Monotheism or polytheism?
Outside observers once called ATR polytheistic. Many African scholars reply that believers hold to one Supreme Being, with the divinities as His servants, and some, such as Idowu, describe this as diffused monotheism.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a short question asks who or what, or asks for two or three functions.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give the fact first (for example that the divinities derive from the Supreme Being), then one sentence of explanation for each point; do not simply list names.

variantes.nom: Discuss a quotation (for example that divinity is well stratified)
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a statement about the structure of belief is given and you must test it.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Define the term, show the levels with their roles, show how authority passes downward, then note where beliefs differ between peoples and conclude.

sections.enonce_markdown: 'Africans who follow their traditional religion worship many gods.' Discuss.

etapes.action: Analyse the command word and the claim.
etapes.justification: 'Discuss' means the claim must be tested, not accepted or rejected at once.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Plan: (1) why the claim seems true, (2) why believers reject it, (3) judgement.

etapes.action: Explain why the claim seems true.
etapes.justification: A fair answer shows the evidence behind the view.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Believers honour many divinities and spirits, each with shrines, priests and festivals, which an outsider may read as many gods.

etapes.justification: Their view is the main evidence on what ATR teaches.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Believers hold that one Supreme Being created all; the divinities owe their origin to Him and act as His agents, so worship ultimately reaches God.

etapes.justification: Showing awareness of difference between peoples is a mark of a strong answer.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Names and emphases differ: among some peoples the divinities are very prominent, among others the Supreme Being is more central.

etapes.justification: The judgement must follow from the discussion.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The claim is partly true of outward practice but, on the believers' own account, misleading about belief.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Model answer, key points:** ATR has many divinities and spirits, so the charge of 'many gods' is understandable; yet believers hold to one Supreme Being from whom the divinities derive their existence and authority, so many scholars describe ATR as belief in one God approached through intermediaries.

items.pourquoi_faux: It misrepresents the believers' view, which treats objects and shrines as symbols or places through which spiritual beings are approached.
items.correction_markdown: Write that believers use objects and shrines as means of approach and as symbols, not that the object itself is God.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing about divinities and ancestors as if they were the same.
items.pourquoi_faux: Divinities are spiritual beings from the Supreme Being; ancestors are departed members of a family or lineage.
items.correction_markdown: Keep the levels separate: Supreme Being, divinities, spirits, ancestors, each with its own role.

items.pourquoi_faux: Chukwu is an Igbo name; other peoples use other names.
items.correction_markdown: Say that peoples have different names for the Supreme Being and give one as an example only.

items.erreur_markdown: 'Africans used to believe in a Supreme Being.'
items.pourquoi_faux: The past tense suggests that ATR is dead, whereas many people still practise it.
items.correction_markdown: Use the present tense: believers in ATR hold, believers say.

items.enonce_markdown: State three attributes ascribed to the Supreme Being in African Traditional Religion.
items.solution_markdown: Award one mark for each attribute correctly stated, for example creator, all-powerful, all-knowing, eternal, just, source of life. **Any three correct attributes.**

items.enonce_markdown: Explain two functions of the divinities in an African community.
items.solution_markdown:
Award a mark for naming and a mark for explaining each function.

- Intermediaries: they carry the needs of people to the Supreme Being and make His power felt.
- Guardians of morality: wrongdoing is believed to offend them, so they help keep order.
- Controllers of natural forces: rain, rivers and the earth on which farming depends.

**Any two functions, each explained.**

items.enonce_markdown: Account for the fact that in many African societies the Supreme Being has few shrines and priests while the divinities have many.
items.solution_markdown:
Award marks for reasons, with the believers' perspective.

- The Supreme Being is seen as high above and beyond full understanding, so people approach Him through intermediaries.
- The divinities are linked to concrete areas of life (farming, healing, rivers), so people need regular ritual with them.
- Divinities are believed to be His agents, so honouring them is a way of reaching Him.
- Prayer to the Supreme Being is still made directly, especially in crisis.

**Judgement:** the difference reflects the roles in the structure, not a lesser importance of the Supreme Being.

items_markdown: ATR is a family of traditional religions; answers must generalise carefully and avoid claiming that one people's belief is all Africa's.
The order is: Supreme Being, divinities, spirits, ancestors; this ordering is what 'stratified' means.
Believers hold that the divinities owe their origin to the Supreme Being and act as His agents.
Divinities are often tied to nature or to human activities and have shrines, priests and festivals.
Scholars debate whether ATR is polytheistic; many describe it as one God approached through intermediaries.
